title: {{NAME}} and the Stampede Cup
moral: A team that lifts each other up can outrun any rival.

pages.content: The Stampede Cup was the greatest soccer tournament in the known world, held every seven years in the Valley of Roaring Stones, where the natural rock walls formed a stadium a thousand years before any human thought to build one. {{NAME}} had arrived with the Wildmane United squad: a cheetah named Zara whose speed made defenders look like they were running through treacle, a rhinoceros defender called Holt who had never, not once, let a striker past him, and their captain, a silver-furred wolf named Atlas, who played with a calm so complete it was almost frightening. {{NAME}} himself had just been offered a place on the team after Atlas saw him score from forty metres with a left foot strike in a practice game that had stopped everyone, including Holt, who claimed to be unimpressible. The stands were already full. The opposing team, the Talonstrike Falcons, warmed up across the pitch in sleek scarlet kits, their eyes golden and razor-sharp.

pages.content: {{NAME}} had a power that none of the other players on the field possessed, though he rarely thought of it that way. He could sense, with strange and uncanny accuracy, where every player on the pitch was about to move, a fraction of a second before they moved. It was not quite flying, not quite reading minds. It was more like hearing the game as a piece of music, and knowing the next note before it came. Atlas had spotted this in the practice match. 'You see the whole board,' the wolf had told him, in that steady low voice of his. 'Most players see only the piece in front of them.' The Talonstrike captain was a falcon named Crest who could cover the full length of the pitch in under three seconds when she spread her wings mid-sprint. She was watching {{NAME}} now from across the halfway line with the focused calculation of a chess player. {{NAME}} met her golden eyes and felt the familiar shiver of a game that was going to require every scrap of everything he had.

pages.content: The first half was ferocious. Zara blurred down the flank twice, only for the Falcon defence to close her off with a precision that was almost supernatural. Holt held the back line like a stone wall, but the Falcons chipped passes over him with aerial ease that a ground-bound rhino simply could not counter. At half time: nil-nil, and everyone breathing hard. {{NAME}} paced the dressing room, that music-sense churning in his chest. The pattern was there, he could feel it. Crest always dropped her left shoulder before striking. Their left midfielder always cut inside rather than outside when under pressure. He told Atlas. The wolf listened with those pale, steady eyes, then stood and addressed the team in a voice that was quiet but that somehow filled every corner of the room. 'Do what {{NAME}} says,' he said. 'Exactly. No improvising.' Zara looked surprised. Holt cracked his knuckles. {{NAME}} felt the weight of it, the trust the wolf had just placed on his shoulders, and stood a little straighter.

pages.content: The second half changed. {{NAME}} fed Zara through the exact gap he had predicted, a sliver between two defenders that lasted less than a second. She hit it perfectly. One-nil. Crest dropped her shoulder and {{NAME}} was already moving, intercepting the ball before it reached her, turning and slipping it to Atlas who drove it hard into the far corner with the kind of unhurried accuracy that made the goalkeeper look like a spectator. Two-nil. The rock-wall crowd erupted, a sound that was less like cheering and more like weather. Crest found {{NAME}} after the final whistle, her golden eyes no longer calculating but genuinely warm. 'You hear it too, don't you?' she said. 'The pattern.' {{NAME}} looked at her, surprised. She dipped her sleek head. 'Most players never hear it.' She offered her wing. He shook it. The Stampede Cup was a battered bronze thing, much smaller than he'd imagined, and it weighed almost nothing. But when Atlas placed it in {{NAME}}'s hands, it felt heavier than anything he had ever held.

pages.content: Later, when the valley had quieted and the stars were out above the rock walls, the Wildmane United team sat together in the long grass of the pitch, passing a flask of warm berry tea around the circle. Holt, it turned out, made terrible but enthusiastic jokes. Zara laughed at all of them too loudly. Atlas sat with his silver tail curled around his paws, looking at the stars with an expression of deep, private contentment. {{NAME}} lay on his back in the grass, the bronze cup on his chest, and listened to the night. The rock walls still hummed faintly with the vibration of all those thousands of cheering feet. He could feel it through the ground, a distant, steady heartbeat. He thought about Crest's question, whether he heard the pattern, and realised that tonight the whole world felt like music played just right. He was asleep before the flask had gone all the way around the circle. And somewhere in the grass, he was certain, something else was beginning. Some new pattern, just at the edge of hearing.
